content: Halogens, also known as halogen elements, are a group of nonmetal elements located in Group 17 of the periodic table (previously referred to as Group VII or VIIA). This group includes fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I), and astatine (At). Additionally, the yet-to-be-discovered element 117, temporarily named ununseptium, is considered a potential member of this group. Halogens are unique in that they are the only group in the periodic table to include elements that exist in all three familiar states of matter—solid, liquid, and gas—under standard temperature and pressure conditions. Due to their high reactivity, halogens are not found in their elemental forms in nature. Instead, they are typically present as compounds or ions. Halide ions and oxoanions, such as iodate (IO₃⁻), are commonly found in minerals and seawater. Halogenated organic compounds, which occur naturally in some living organisms, are also a source of halogens. In their elemental forms, halogens exist as diatomic molecules (e.g., F₂, Cl₂), but these forms are rare in nature and are more commonly encountered in laboratory or industrial settings. At room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, and iodine and astatine are solids. This makes Group 17 the only group in the periodic table to exhibit all three states of matter at room temperature. The term halogen originates from 18th-century scientific French nomenclature, which was derived from Greek roots. The word combines hals (meaning sea or salt) and gen (meaning to generate), referring to elements that produce salts when combined with metals. Halogens exhibit several trends as one moves down the group in the periodic table. These include decreasing electronegativity and reactivity, as well as increasing melting and boiling points. The properties of ununseptium, which has not yet been discovered, are either unknown or estimated based on the behavior of similar elements. Halogens are highly reactive, which can make them harmful or even lethal to biological organisms in sufficient quantities. This reactivity arises from their atomic structure, as halogen atoms are one electron short of a full outer shell of eight electrons. They achieve stability by reacting with atoms of other elements to gain this missing electron. Fluorine is the most reactive element known, capable of attacking even inert materials like glass and forming compounds with heavier noble gases. It is a corrosive and highly toxic gas. In laboratory settings, fluorine can react with glass in the presence of small amounts of water to form silicon tetrafluoride (SiF₄). As a result, fluorine must be handled with materials such as Teflon, extremely dry glass, or metals like copper or steel, which form a protective fluoride layer on their surfaces. Chlorine and bromine are widely used as disinfectants for drinking water, swimming pools, fresh wounds, dishes, and surfaces. They kill bacteria and other harmful microorganisms through sterilization. These halogens are also used in bleaching processes. For example, sodium hypochlorite, derived from chlorine, is the active ingredient in most fabric bleaches and is used in the production of some paper products. All halogens form binary compounds with hydrogen, known as hydrogen halides (e.g., HF, HCl, HBr, HI). These compounds are strong acids when dissolved in water, where they are referred to as hydrohalic acids. Hydrastatic acid (HAt), derived from astatine, could theoretically qualify as a hydrohalic acid, but it is rarely discussed due to astatine's extreme instability and tendency to undergo alpha decay. Halogens can also react with each other to form interhalogen compounds, such as bromine monofluoride (BrF), iodine monochloride (ICl), and chlorine monofluoride (ClF). These compounds share some similarities with the pure halogens but often exhibit intermediate properties between their parent halogens. For example, while chlorine (Cl₂) and iodine (I₂) are soluble in carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄), iodine monochloride (ICl) is not, as it is a polar molecule due to the significant electronegativity difference between iodine and chlorine. Many synthetic organic compounds, such as plastic polymers, and some natural compounds contain halogen atoms. These are referred to as halogenated compounds or organic halides. Chlorine is the most abundant halogen and the only one required in relatively large amounts by humans, primarily as chloride ions. Chloride ions play a critical role in brain function by mediating the action of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and are also used by the body to produce stomach acid. Iodine is required in trace amounts for the synthesis of thyroid hormones, such as thyroxine. In contrast, fluorine and bromine are not considered essential for humans, although small amounts of fluoride can strengthen tooth enamel and make it resistant to decay. In drug discovery, incorporating halogen atoms into a lead drug candidate can result in analogues that are more lipophilic and less water-soluble. This property enhances the drug's ability to penetrate lipid membranes. However, halogenated drugs have a tendency to accumulate in lipid tissues, which can be undesirable. The chemical reactivity of halogen atoms depends on their point of attachment to the lead compound and the specific halogen involved. Aromatic halogen groups are generally less reactive than aliphatic halogen groups, which can exhibit significant chemical reactivity. Among aliphatic carbon-halogen bonds, the carbon-fluorine (C-F) bond is the strongest and typically less reactive than aliphatic carbon-hydrogen (C-H) bonds. The other aliphatic carbon-halogen bonds are weaker, with reactivity increasing down the periodic table. Consequently, the most commonly used halogen substitutions in drug design are the less reactive aromatic fluorine and chlorine groups.
